n: The ark stays in Philistine territory for seven months, a long stretch of suffering for them and of mourning for Israel.
The Philistines consult their religious experts about how to return the ark properly.

f.g: people who claimed to discover hidden knowledge through omens and magic

n: The priests advise sending a gift to make amends. Then they will be healed, or at least learn whether Israel's God was truly the cause.

f.g: Also called a guilt offering — a payment to make up for a wrong done.

n: The offering is to be five golden tumors and five golden mice, one for each Philistine ruler, since all five cities suffered the same plague.

f.g: Mice or rats may have spread the plague, which some scholars think was bubonic.

n: Making gold images of the plague was a way of sending the trouble away and of giving glory to Israel's God. Even pagans could recognize the Lord's power.

f.w: give glory unto the God of Israel

n: The priests warn the people not to be stubborn like Pharaoh. They knew the story of the Exodus — God's power against Egypt had become famous.

f.w: as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts

n: They set up a test: a new cart pulled by two nursing cows that have never been yoked, with their calves penned at home. Naturally, such cows would turn back toward their calves.

f.g: never trained to pull a cart

n: The ark goes on the cart, with the gold offerings in a box beside it, and the cows are to be released to go wherever they will.
If the cows head straight toward Beth-shemesh in Israel, it proves Israel's God sent the plagues. If not, it was just bad luck.

f.g: An Israelite town on the border with Philistia, assigned to the priests.

n: The Philistines follow the plan exactly, hitching up the cows and penning in their calves.
They place the ark and the box of golden images on the cart.
Against all natural instinct, the cows go straight to Beth-shemesh, mooing for their calves but never turning aside. The Philistine rulers follow them to the border and see God's hand clearly.
The people of Beth-shemesh are harvesting wheat in the valley when they look up and see the ark coming home. Their joy is great.
The cart stops by a large stone in Joshua's field. The people chop up the cart for firewood and sacrifice the cows to the Lord as a burnt offering.
Levites, the tribe authorized to handle the ark, lift it and the gold box onto the stone. The town offers sacrifices in thanksgiving.

f.w: the Levites took down the ark

n: Having seen everything, the five Philistine rulers return to Ekron the same day, convinced.
The narrator lists the five golden tumors: one for each major Philistine city — Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron.

f.g: Ashkelon, a Philistine city on the coast.

n: The golden mice represented all the Philistine towns, fortified cities and villages alike. The great stone where the ark rested remained as a landmark when this was written.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “the great stone” (Hebrew ’eben) rather than Abel.

n: Some men of Beth-shemesh look inside the ark — something forbidden even to Levites — and are struck down. The number in the text is very large; many scholars think a copying error inflated it, as some manuscripts read seventy.

f.w: they had looked into the ark
fifty thousand and threescore and ten men
f.g: Literally “seventy men, fifty thousand men”; the historian Josephus mentions seventy.

n: Shaken, the townspeople ask who can stand before such a holy God. They learn that God's holiness must be approached with reverence, not curiosity.

f.w: Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?

n: They send messengers to Kirjath-jearim, a town farther inland, asking its people to come take the ark.

f.g: “Town of forests,” a few miles west of Jerusalem; the ark stayed there about twenty years.
